lesson.title: Multiplying Polynomials: The Area Trick

steps.say: Hey, so picture this. You've got a community garden plot out in Surrey, and the city needs to know the area to figure out how much compost to order. The plot's length is x plus four metres and the width is x plus two metres. You can't just write 'x plus four times x plus two' and hand it in — you actually need to multiply those two expressions together and simplify. That's what multiplying polynomials is, and I promise it's way more like a recipe than a mystery.

visual.caption: Your garden plot: length (x + 4) m, width (x + 2) m — find the area

steps.say: Here's the whole trick, and it's the exact same idea you used with 23 times 15 in, I don't know, Grade 6. You split each side into its pieces, then multiply every piece on one side by every piece on the other side, and add up all the little rectangle areas. For 23 times 15 you get 20 by 10, 20 by 5, 3 by 10, and 3 by 5. For polynomials it's the same four-pair pattern: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second bracket. That's the distributive property, and honestly, that's the entire method.

visual.caption: 23 × 15 splits into four pieces — exactly the same shape as two binomials

steps.say: Alright, let's do (x plus four) times (x plus two) together, slowly. Pair one: x times x, that's x squared. Pair two: x times 2, that's 2x. Pair three: 4 times x, that's 4x. Pair four: 4 times 2, that's 8. Now line them all up: x squared, plus 2x, plus 4x, plus 8. Spot those middle two? 2x and 4x are like terms, so they add to 6x. You're left with x squared plus 6x plus 8. That's your area, and that's your answer.

visual.caption: Four partial products x², 2x, 4x, 8 combine into x² + 6x + 8

steps.say: Now let's crank it up a notch. What about (2x plus 3) times (x plus 1)? Same recipe, no different steps. 2x times x gives you 2x squared. 2x times 1 gives you 2x. 3 times x gives you 3x. 3 times 1 gives you 3. Add them all: 2x squared plus 2x plus 3x plus 3. Combine the x terms — 2x plus 3x is 5x — and you get 2x squared plus 5x plus 3. Notice how the 2 in front of x carried through to give you 2x squared? That's the one spot students trip on, so keep an eye on your leading coefficients.

Okay, last one and it's a little bigger: a trinomial times a binomial. You're expanding (x plus 2) times (x squared plus 3x plus 1). The rule hasn't changed — every term in the first bracket still hits every term in the second. So x times x squared is x cubed. x times 3x is 3x squared. x times 1 is x. Then 2 times x squared is 2x squared, 2 times 3x is 6x, and 2 times 1 is 2. Now combine: x cubed, plus 3x squared plus 2x squared is 5x squared, plus x plus 6x is 7x, plus 2. Done: x cubed plus 5x squared plus 7x plus 2. See, it's just more pairs. The method never changes.

So here's your one-sentence cheat sheet for the whole lesson: to multiply two polynomials, every term in the first one multiplies every term in the second one, then you combine like terms. Whether it's two binomials, a trinomial and a binomial, or a monster with five terms, it's the same loop. You've basically just been doing 23 times 15 the whole time — you just swapped the digits for x's.
steps.math: (\text{1st bracket})\times(\text{2nd bracket}) = \text{sum of all term-pair products, like terms combined}

steps.say: Quick check for yourself before you close the book: you're building a raised bed for the school garden. The length is (3x plus 2) metres and the width is (x plus 5) metres. Write the area as a single polynomial in x. Give it a shot, then peek at the answer below.

visual.caption: School garden bed: (3x + 2) m by (x + 5) m

lesson.answer: Multiply every term in the first polynomial by every term in the second, then combine like terms — it's just the distributive property, no matter how many terms you've got.

practice.question: You're tiling a rectangular patio in your condo's courtyard. The length is (4x + 3) metres and the width is (2x + 1) metre. Write the area of the patio as a single polynomial in x (in square metres).
